analysis.one_liner: Exempts estates worth up to $7.5 million from the estate tax and caps rates at 30 percent.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2003 with zero cosponsors, the bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee and died without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let every estate pass up to $7.5 million tax-free — far above the $1 million exemption in effect at the time — and taxed whatever remained at 25 percent, with a 30 percent rate only on amounts above $50 million. It also would have canceled the 2001 tax law's scheduled repeal of the estate and gift tax after 2009, keeping a much-reduced version of the tax on the books permanently. Rep. Harold Ford Jr., a Democrat, introduced it with no cosponsors; the House tax-writing committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates worth more than $1 million. Estates up to $7.5 million would owe nothing, and the largest fortunes would see their federal rate fall to 25-30 percent from a top rate of 49 percent. The families with fortunes above $50 million would give up the scheduled 2010 full repeal and instead pay a permanent, much lower tax.

how_it_helps.text: Estates would owe no federal estate tax up to an exclusion of $7.5 million, several times the $1 million exemption in effect when the bill was introduced.

The tax rate on taxable estates would drop to 25 percent, rising to 30 percent only on amounts above $50 million — far below the top rate of 49 percent then in effect under the 2001 tax law's phase-down.

The bill would cancel the provisions of the 2001 law scheduled to repeal the estate and gift tax after December 31, 2009, replacing a one-year full repeal (followed by the tax snapping back at old, higher levels) with a permanent low-rate tax on large estates.
The changes would take effect for deaths and gifts after December 31, 2003.

analysis.who_pays: The federal budget. The estate tax is paid only by the estates of the largest fortunes, so cutting it saves most families nothing directly — the lost revenue would be made up through other taxes, borrowing, or lower public spending, borne by everyone else.

drawbacks.text: Exempting everything under $7.5 million and capping rates at 25-30 percent would give up most of the revenue the estate tax raises, shifting the cost to other taxpayers or the deficit.

By repealing the scheduled post-2009 repeal of the estate and gift tax, the bill would impose a permanent federal tax of 25-30 percent at death on the largest fortunes — the outcome that full-repeal supporters wanted to avoid, so the bill served neither side fully.
The giveaway to heirs of estates between $1 million and $7.5 million would be permanent law, with no offsetting revenue anywhere in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded away most of the estate tax to preserve a slice of it. The genuine upside was certainty: instead of the 2001 law's schedule — a shrinking tax, one year of full repeal in 2010, then the old high rates snapping back in 2011 — the largest estates would have faced a simple, permanent 25-30 percent levy. The cost is that every estate above $1 million would have gained enormously at the Treasury's expense, with the burden landing on general taxpayers. As a tax cut for the wealthy it was sweeping; as a compromise to save the tax from full repeal it was a deliberate half-measure. It never advanced far enough for anyone to have to defend that trade.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled any action on it, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Harold Ford Jr., a Democrat, introduced the bill on June 16, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The bill would have exempted estates up to $7.5 million, taxed the remainder at 25 percent (30 percent above $50 million), and canceled the 2001 law's scheduled estate and gift tax repeal after 2009.
Not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.
The Ways and Means Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Treasury and anyone counting on the estate tax's revenue: because the bill went nowhere, the tax stayed as it stood — a $1 million exemption with top rates scheduled to fall to 45 percent — rather than being permanently reset at $7.5 million and 25-30 percent. Nobody had to spend anything to stop it; it simply never attracted support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Harold Ford Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 16, 2003; attracted no cosponsors and the bill never advanced past referral.

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 16, 2003 and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the referral; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote and drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split was ever measured; the sponsor was a Democrat and the committee that held it had a Republican majority.

industries.note: Estates between the then-current $1 million exemption and $7.5 million would have owed nothing, and the biggest fortunes' rate would have fallen to 25-30 percent from as high as 49 percent. The gain comes entirely out of federal revenue that everyone else's taxes fund. (Families above $50 million would have lost the scheduled 2010 full repeal, but paid far less than the old 55 percent top rate.)

A $7.5 million exemption would spare family farms and businesses under that line from any estate tax and from pressure to sell assets to pay it. The cost shows up as lost public revenue rather than on the businesses' own books.

A $7.5 million exemption would erase the need for tax-driven planning for all but the largest estates, but canceling the 2010 sunset keeps a permanent tax — and steady planning demand — for fortunes above that line.
